settings.heading: Sublimation vs HTV
settings.answer: Sublimation vs HTV splits on fabric: sublimation dyes the design into light-colored polyester permanently with zero hand feel, while HTV is cut vinyl pressed on top — it works on any fabric and any color, including cotton and darks. Poly and performance blanks go sublimation; cotton, darks, and simple text go HTV.

settings.text: Fabric decides it: sublimation only bonds to polyester — roughly 65% poly or higher, and the higher the poly, the brighter the print. HTV works on cotton, poly, blends, even nylon.
Garment color is the second gate: sublimation dyes are transparent, so they only show on white and light garments. HTV is opaque vinyl — darks are no problem.

Durability goes to sublimation: the dye becomes part of the fiber, so it won't crack or peel and lasts the life of the garment. HTV sits on top and is typically rated around 50 washes applied correctly.
Feel goes to sublimation too: zero hand — the fabric stays exactly as soft as it started. HTV adds a vinyl layer you can feel, and stacked colors add stiffness.
HTV starts cheaper: an entry cutter (~$200–500) plus a heat press. Sublimation needs a sublimation printer — entry setups run roughly $300–500 — plus sublimation paper and a press.
The blank is the same flat 99¢ a unit either way — athletic jerseys and poly performance tees for sublimation, cotton crews for HTV, every size one price.

settings.heading: Dye Job vs Vinyl
settings.intro: Both methods end at a heat press, but they put ink in very different places. Sublimation turns dye to gas and bonds it inside polyester fibers; HTV is a solid sheet of vinyl cut to shape and pressed onto the surface. Here's how they stack up.

settings.blurb: A lightweight poly performance tee — sublimation's home turf. The dye bonds into the knit with zero hand feel; the space-dye heather adds texture under an all-over print, and lighter panels print truest.
An adult sleeveless jersey in a lightweight athletic knit — the garment class sublimation was built for. Full-bleed team designs go sublimation; single-color HTV numbers press on either way.
A sleeveless athletic jersey in an Athletic Red/Black/White colorway through 3XL — HTV territory. Opaque vinyl doesn't care about the red and black panels; names and numbers press in one layer.
A smooth cotton crew with the deepest stock on the floor. Cotton is where sublimation taps out and HTV shines — vinyl grips it predictably, wash after wash.

settings.question: Is sublimation better than HTV?
settings.answer: Neither is universally better — the blank decides. On white or light polyester, sublimation wins: unlimited colors, zero hand feel, and a print that lasts the life of the garment. On cotton, blends, or dark garments, HTV is the practical choice — it's opaque, works on almost any fabric, and starts on cheaper equipment. Poly athletic wear goes sublimation; cotton and darks go HTV.

settings.question: Why doesn't sublimation work on cotton or dark shirts?
settings.answer: Sublimation dye bonds to polyester molecules under heat — cotton fibers have nothing for it to grab, so prints on cotton wash out and fade fast. And because sublimation dyes are transparent with no white ink, they're invisible on dark fabric. The workaround for cotton is sublimation-coated HTV: a printable white vinyl you sublimate onto, then press to the garment — but at that point you're layering vinyl anyway.

settings.question: Which lasts longer, sublimation or HTV?
settings.answer: Sublimation. The dye becomes part of the fiber itself, so there's nothing on the surface to crack, peel, or flake — the print typically lasts as long as the garment does. HTV sits on top of the fabric and is generally rated around 50 washes when applied at the right time, temperature, and pressure; edges and layered designs can lift sooner as the vinyl ages.

settings.question: What equipment do you need for sublimation vs HTV?
settings.answer: For HTV: a vinyl cutter (entry machines run roughly $200–500) and a heat press. For sublimation: a sublimation printer — entry setups built on converted inkjets run roughly $300–500, dedicated machines more — plus sublimation paper and a heat press. HTV is the cheaper door into the craft; sublimation pays off in durability and full-color range once you're printing poly regularly.

settings.question: What temperature and time do sublimation and HTV press at?
settings.answer: Sublimation runs hot and long: roughly 385–400°F for 40–60 seconds, which is what turns the dye to gas so it bonds into the polyester. HTV runs cooler and quicker: roughly 305–320°F for 10–15 seconds for standard vinyl, with low-temp formulas made for heat-sensitive synthetics. Always follow the specific transfer or vinyl maker's settings over any generic chart.

settings.question: What blanks should I buy for sublimation or HTV?
settings.answer: For sublimation: light-colored polyester — athletic jerseys and performance tees are the classic canvas. For HTV: nearly anything, with smooth cotton crews the most forgiving surface. Buying by the pack at a flat 99¢ a unit keeps test presses cheap, and every size in the run costs the same.
